bib.title: Graph Machine Learning in the Era of Large Language Models (LLMs)
bib.venue: preprint (arXiv v3, 29 May 2026; ACM template, J. ACM Vol. 37 No. 4 Article 0)

read.skipped: Reference list (about 2400 of 2911 lines onward) skimmed for arXiv ids only; body, tables and review-methodology section read in full.

question: How are LLMs used to improve Graph ML (features, label scarcity, heterophily/OOD, trustworthiness) and how are graphs, especially KGs, used to improve LLMs?
contributions: We detail the evolution from early graph learning methods to the latest Graph ML in the era of LLMs;
We provide a comprehensive analysis of current LLMs enhanced Graph ML methods, highlighting their advantages and limitations, and offering a systematic categorization;
We thoroughly investigate the potential of graph structures to address the limitations of LLMs;
We explore the applications and prospective future directions of Graph ML in the era of LLMs, and discuss both research and practical applications in various fields.

results.claim: OFA, using LLM-generated feature embeddings, beats the best GNN (GCN) on Citeseer in accuracy.
results.source: OFA (Liu et al. 2023, arXiv:2310.00149), as summarised in Sec 4.5.2
results.setup: Citeseer; OFA with LLM feature embeddings vs best GNN-based model GCN; survey does not state whether points or relative
results.quote: improvements of 3.20% in accuracy and 3.49% in F1 score on the Citeseer dataset
results.note: F1 improvement 3.49% in the same sentence.

results.claim: LLM-as-enhancer is cheaper than iterative LLM-GNN training: TAPE (frozen LLM, only GNN updated) is faster than GLEM with the same backbones.
results.source: TAPE (He et al. 2023) vs GLEM (Zhao et al. 2022), as summarised in Sec 4.5.1
results.setup: same backbone models; LLM fixed during training in TAPE, GLEM alternates LLM and GNN updates
results.quote: TAPE achieves a notable speedup—e.g., a 2.88× improvement—even when using the same backbone models

results.claim: LLM-as-predictor GraphText takes orders of magnitude longer to train than GCN on Cora.
results.quote: had a training time exceeding 103 seconds, while a standard GCN required only about 10 seconds
results.note: Text extraction prints '103'; likely 10^3 with lost superscript, unverified.

results.claim: LLMs as feature enhancers generally improve downstream performance, while LLMs as direct predictors sometimes underperform GNNs.
results.source: Chen et al. 2023 (arXiv:2307.03393) and GLBench (Li et al. 2024)
results.setup: node classification benchmarks on text-attributed graphs
results.quote: LLMs used as direct predictors sometimes underperform compared to traditional GNN models

results.claim: No clear evidence that larger LLMs consistently help on graph tasks.
results.source: Chen et al. 2023; Li et al. 2024
results.quote: there is no clear evidence that increasing the size of LLM parameters consistently leads to better performance on graph tasks

results.claim: Describing graph structure in text is limited by context length and needs per-dataset prompt engineering that does not transfer; this motivates GNN-encoded (explicit) structure.
results.setup: implicit structural information methods (GPT4Graph, NLGraph, GraphText etc.)
results.quote: LLMs can only get local structural information, and lengthy contexts might diminish their reasoning

results.claim: Guo et al. report that both LLM-as-enhancer and LLM-as-predictor improve robustness over shallow models under structural (PGD) and textual (SemAttack) attacks.
results.setup: citation graphs; no numbers given in the survey
results.quote: both approaches significantly improve robustness compared to traditional shallow models

results.claim: InstructGLM builds 31 instruction prompts from four configuration parameters.
results.setup: Flan-T5 instruction tuning; params: task type, node features included, max hop order, node connections used
results.quote: They generate a set of 31 prompts by combining four configuration parameters

results.claim: OFA collects nine text-attributed graph datasets to train one cross-domain graph classifier.
results.setup: nodes and relations described in natural language, embedded by an LLM into one space
results.quote: OFA collects nine text-attributed graph datasets covering diverse domains

limits: The survey runs no experiments; every number is quoted from other work and most method comparisons are qualitative.
Authors concede many studies give no efficiency comparison, so the performance/cost trade-off is hard to assess (Sec 4.5.1).
Authors say KG-enhanced LLM pre-training research is limited, so they also cover KG-enhanced PLMs (Sec 5.1).
Graph transformers: quadratic self-attention cost and possible loss of structure when serialising the graph (Sec 3.1.2).

Listed open problems: graph RAG efficiency on large graphs, cross-domain graph generalisation, trustworthiness (robustness, explainability, fairness, privacy), API cost of GPT-4 on large graphs, multi-modal graphs (Sec 7).
Table 2 is a coverage table, not a results table; datasets are shown as counts and symbols (symbols lost in text extraction).
Robot planning: search space grows explosively with task complexity (Sec 6.4).
Review scope: 2018 to 2025, top venues plus arXiv and OpenReview preprints (Sec 9).
practices: Use an LLM as a feature enhancer (text encoder, or generator of labels/explanations/descriptions) feeding a GNN predictor; the survey says this is the more effective and balanced strategy than LLM as direct predictor (Sec 4.5.2).
Keep the LLM frozen when only features are needed: efficiency loss is minimal (TAPE) versus joint LLM-GNN training such as GLEM (Sec 4.5.1).

When feeding a graph to an LLM, choose among ignoring structure (reduces to text classification), implicit structure in text (neighbour lists, retrieval-based prompts, structured languages such as GraphML, graph syntax trees) or explicit structure (GNN encoder + fusion + LLM) (Sec 4.2).
For explicit structure use encoding, fusion and LLM modules; a linear projector to soft prompts is the simple fusion, Q-Former style GIT-Former is the heavier option (Sec 4.2.3).
For large graphs retrieve a query-relevant subgraph first (G-Retriever) rather than serialising everything (Sec 4.2.3, 7.1).
Prefer KG integration at inference (ICL or fine-tuned adapters/soft prompts) over pre-training when knowledge must stay current, since KGs update cheaply (Sec 5.2).
Convert KG triples to natural language before prompting, since raw (head, relation, tail) triples may not be understood well (Wu et al., Sec 5.2.1).
Use parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA, QLoRA) and pruning to reduce LLM cost on graph tasks (Sec 7.4).
Adapt pre-trained GNNs by unsupervised representation learning, fine-tuning (AdapterGNN for parameter-efficient) or prompt tuning, which keeps the GNN frozen (Sec 3.2.2, Fig 4).
